title: Ncha
author: Chidinma Eze
desc: The palm-oil-and-alkali emulsion that underlies abacha, nkwobi, isi ewu and ugba — half a cup of oil to two teaspoons of potash dissolved in a quarter cup of water, stirred until it emulsifies.
longDesc: Ncha is not a dish, it is the technique that several southeastern dishes are built on, and it is worth knowing by name. Palm oil is mixed with ground ehuru, crayfish, seasoning, scotch bonnet and onion; potash is dissolved separately in water and sieved so no sediment goes in; then the potash water is poured slowly into the oil while stirring until the whole thing emulsifies and turns from red liquid to thick yellow paste. That same emulsion dresses African salad, coats cow foot in nkwobi and goat head in isi ewu. One sauce, four dishes.
ingredients: 2 tsp potash (akanwu), dissolved in 1/4 cup water and sieved
steps: Combine the palm oil with the ehuru, crayfish, seasoning, scotch bonnet and chopped onions in a clean dry bowl.
Dissolve the potash in the quarter cup of water and sieve it, leaving the sediment behind.
Pour the potash mix slowly into the palm oil mix, stirring continuously.
Keep stirring until your sauce is emulsified — it will go from red and liquid to thick and yellow.
Fold in the ugba and the chopped scent leaf.
Use at once to dress abacha, nkwobi or isi ewu.
chefTips: A clean dry bowl. Water in the vessel breaks the emulsion before it forms, which is exactly why abacha is mixed off the stove.
Sieve the potash water and leave the sediment. The undissolved particles are gritty and taste harsh.
Pour slowly, stir continuously. Dumped in, the alkali does not disperse and you get a split sauce with yellow lumps in it.
Thick, not fluid, is the target. If it is still pourable you have added too much potash water.
The colour change is the cue and it is unmistakable — red oil turns opaque yellow and thickens visibly.
Two teaspoons of potash to half a cup of oil is the only clean oil-to-alkali ratio found in any named source. Use it as your starting point.
This same emulsion goes by other names: Sisi Jemimah calls hers Ngo sauce (NGA059), and All Nigerian Recipes describes the identical process without naming it at all.
commonMistakes: Pouring the potash water in all at once.
Adding too much potash water, so it stays liquid.
Warming it, which is unnecessary and can break it.
sources: Adapted from 'Ncha – Nkwobi Sauce', byline 'afrolems'. Quantities as printed: 1/2 cup Palm oil; 2 tsps Potash mixed with 1/4 cup water, dissolved and sieved; 1 tsp Ehuru powder; 1 tsp Seasoning powder; 2.25 tsps Crayfish powder; Scotch bonnet to taste; 1 tablespoon Ugba; 1 tablespoon chopped scent leaf; 1 tablespoon chopped onions; salt to taste. Yield not specified.
This is the ONLY clean oil-to-alkali ratio found in any source consulted for the ncha emulsion.

THE CROSS-DISH CLAIM, in print from a named source, and the reason this has its own entry: the page defines ncha as 'the rich palm oil based emulsion that coats the gelatinous cowlegs, goat meat or "biscuit bone"' and states that 'Ncha is the base for a number of south eastern dishes', also naming its use as a dressing for African Salad. That single sentence spans nkwobi and isi ewu (cowleg, goat meat) and abacha (African Salad).

The method is as printed: 'Pour in the potash mix slowly into the palm oil mix and keep stirring until your sauce is emulsified'. NOTE that its only doneness cue is 'emulsified', which is weaker than the colour cue given by other sources — All Nigerian Recipes' abacha page says 'Stir very well and you'll see the oil turn into a yellow paste', and its nkwobi page says 'You'll notice the palm oil begin to curdle and turn yellow. Keep stirring till all the oil has turned yellow.' Those colour cues are used in the tips above.

INDEPENDENT ATTESTATION of the name: 1Q Food Platter's abacha page names it explicitly — 'Add 1 ground Uda to the oil and add the soda water stir vigorously using a spoon to form a paste called Ncha' (NGA056).

COUNTER-FINDING, flagged: All Nigerian Recipes does NOT use the word 'ncha' on its African Salad page despite describing the identical process. So the technique is universal but the NAME is not universally printed.

ACADEMIC CORROBORATION of the term, title only: 'Production and evaluation of instant emulsion base (ncha) from oil palm biogenic waste' — the title itself glosses ncha as 'emulsion base'. The paper could not be retrieved (ResearchGate returned 429), so only the title and framing are relied on here.

ON THE ALKALI: potash, baking soda, soda water and plantain-peel ash water are treated as interchangeable for forming ncha across the sources consulted. They are chemically different bases of different strength and NO source quantifies the substitution. That is a real gap. See NGA120 for the chemistry and the safety note.
storage: Use immediately. The emulsion separates within a few hours.
reheating: Do not reheat. Make it fresh.
healthBenefits: Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
Ehuru and scent leaf are traditionally used as digestives.
No cooking at all, so nothing is degraded by heat.
culturalNote: Learning that ncha is a named thing rather than a step changes how the southeastern repertoire reads. Abacha, nkwobi, isi ewu and dressed ugba are not four unrelated dishes but four things you can put the same emulsion on, and the knowledge that matters is the emulsion. The same logic turns up in the Delta, where owo is made creamy by exactly this move.
